paragraphs: Ner shabbat, hachiyyub min haddin hu ner echad, ak "p hassod tzarik lehadliq shette nerot, echad keneged "zakur", veechad keneged "shamur". gam od, hem keneged shene hhy"n deshem hvy"h b"h, shehem sod bina umalkut sheoleh misparam tqs"g keminyan "neheneh mizziv hashshekina". vehamdaqdeqin madliqin shiba nerot, veomerim haolam - keneged z' sepirot chg"t nhy"m haremuzim bashshabua. vaapillu hammadliqin z' nerot, k"z, kesheyyabo lebeto yistakkel bishte nerot davqa, vikavven shehem, echad keneged "zakur" veechad keneged "shamur". gam yekavven: echad keneged he" rishona veechad keneged he" acharona. gam yekavven sheyyairu nerot shebbiqdushsha lemala.

clarification.explanation: According to strict law, it suffices to light one Sabbath candle, but according to the esoteric tradition one must light specifically two candles: one corresponding to the word "Remember" (in the commandment "Remember the Sabbath day") and one to "Observe," and likewise corresponding to the two letters heh of the Name YHVH (symbolizing the sefirot of Binah and Malchut), whose combined numerical value (563) equals the expression "delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah." The most meticulous light seven candles, corresponding to the seven sefirot Chesed-Gevurah-Tiferet-Netzach-Hod-Yesod-Malchut alluded to in the days of the week. But even one who lights seven candles must, upon coming home, look specifically at two candles, intending that one corresponds to "Remember" and one to "Observe," and also to the two letters heh of the Name, and intend that the candles of holiness above shine.
takeaways: The strict-law obligation is one candle; according to the esoteric tradition, two candles (corresponding to "Remember" and "Observe," and the two letters heh of the Name YHVH)
The most meticulous light seven candles, but should always look specifically at two candles and have the proper intention

paragraphs: Iqqar hadlaqat hanner bemaqom sheokel, vaalehem tebarek haishsha hammadleqet et birkat hadlaqat hanner. umikkol maqom tiqqenu chaza"l sheyyadliq ner echad bemaqom sheyyashan sham, veken bebet hattabshil, ubekol maqom sheyyesh lo kenisa bo ballayla lehotzi ulehaknis. bekol meqomot ellu tadliq haishsha belo beraka, veaach"k tadliq bimqom hashshulchan bibraka. veim yirtzeh haish lehadliq bimqom shena beyado, tabo alayv beraka, ak lo yebarek, yaan ki ishto mebareket benerot shel meqom hashshulchan. umi sheen lo maot liqnot shemen shabbat, yachzor al happetachim veyiqneh, ak leadam kazeh saggi ner echad.

clarification.explanation: The primary place for lighting the Sabbath candle is the place of eating (the table), and there the woman recites the blessing over the lighting of the candles. But our Sages enacted that an additional candle also be lit in the sleeping place, and likewise in the kitchen, and in every place one enters and exits at night — except that in all these additional places one lights without a blessing, and the blessing is recited only over the candles of the table. If the husband wants to light a candle himself in the sleeping place, he is permitted to do so and it is good that he do so, but he should not recite a blessing over it, since his wife has already recited the blessing over the candles of the table. One who has no money to buy oil for the Sabbath should ask for charity in order to buy it, but in such a case one candle suffices.
takeaways: The primary candle (with a blessing) is in the place of eating; additional candles in the sleeping place and kitchen are lit without a blessing
One who lacks the means may light with just one candle

paragraphs: Ner shabbat veyayin leqiddush - ner qodem; "p deqiddush deorayeta - yakol leqaddesh min hattora al happat, umiddibre soperim hu detzarik yayin, lepikak ner shabbat qodem mishshum shelom beto; mihu, im yesh lo kede liqnot shemen lener echad ukede yayin leqiddush, abal en lo kede liqnot lener sheni, en lebattel hayyayin bishbil liqnot lener sheni, ki min haddin saggi bener echad.

clarification.explanation: Between the Sabbath candle and the wine for Kiddush, the Sabbath candle takes precedence, even though Kiddush is a Torah obligation (though one can fulfill the Torah obligation of Kiddush even over bread rather than specifically wine; the need for wine is by rabbinic law). The reason the Sabbath candle takes precedence is for the sake of peace in the home (to prevent darkness and strife in the house). Nevertheless, if a person has money to buy oil for one candle and wine for Kiddush, but no more to buy oil for a second candle, he should not forgo buying the wine in order to buy a second candle, since according to strict law one candle suffices.
takeaways: The Sabbath candle takes precedence over the wine of Kiddush, for the sake of peace in the home
With limited resources: buy one candle and wine, and do not give up the wine for a second candle, since one candle suffices by strict law

paragraphs: "p sheokel umeqaddesh al haggag seor hallebana zoreach al shulchano mibbeereb, im kol zeh madliqin ner shabbat bibraka, yaan dener shabbat millebad taam happeshati shel shelom habbayit, yesh bo chiyyub "p hassod, ken heeleti bsh"q "mqbtzl"; veayyen "eshel-abraham", si' rs"g, s"q k"; y"sh.

clarification.explanation: Even if a person eats and recites Kiddush on the roof, where the light of the moon has already been shining on his table since evening (so that he has no practical need for a candle), he must still light the Sabbath candle with a blessing. The reason: the commandment of the Sabbath candle is not only for the plain reason of peace in the home (practical lighting), but carries an additional obligation according to the esoteric tradition, and is therefore required even when there is no actual need for its light.
takeaways: The obligation of the Sabbath candle does not depend only on the practical need for light, but also carries meaning and obligation according to the esoteric tradition — and so it is required even when there is alternative lighting

paragraphs: Echad haish veechad haishsha chayyabim bener shabbat, ella shehaishsha muzheret alayv beyoter, veyesh lah din qedima al balah bimtzuvva zo; veim yirtzeh habbaal lehadliq hu beatzmo, yekola leakkeb beyado; mihu, im yirtzeh habbaal lehadliq bimqom shena – rashshay, velo yebarek, ukemo shekkatabti leel. venahagu beishsha yoledet - madliq habbaal bimqom hashshulchan umebarek, beshabbat rishona sheachar halleda.

clarification.explanation: Both the man and the woman are obligated in the commandment of the Sabbath candle, except that the woman is cautioned about it more, and she has precedence over her husband in fulfilling this commandment. If the husband wants to light it himself (in the place of the table), the woman may prevent him, since the commandment belongs primarily to her. But if the husband wants to light a candle in the sleeping place (the additional candle), he is permitted to do so, and he should not recite a blessing over it, as explained above. A special custom: when a woman has given birth, on the first Sabbath after the birth, it is the husband who lights in the place of the table and recites the blessing, in her place.
takeaways: The woman takes precedence over her husband in the commandment of the Sabbath candle and may prevent him from lighting in the place of the table
On the first Sabbath after childbirth, the husband lights and recites the blessing in the woman's place

paragraphs: Tob shehabbaal yaasoq beereb shabbat betiqqun hannerot, behannachat hashshemen vehappetilot, vekamporash bedibre rabbenu haari"y beseper hakkavvanot vezeh leshono: gam tizzaher betiqqun hannerot shel shabbat; amenam hadlaqat hanner, hi metzuvva al haishsha baalat habbayit kannoda; ad kan leshono; ayyen sham. veken anachnu nohagim bebetenu laarok uletaqqen hannerot beyadenu.

clarification.explanation: It is right and proper that the husband busy himself on the eve of the Sabbath with preparing the candles — arranging the oil and the wicks in advance — as the Ari wrote: one should be careful about preparing the Sabbath candles, even though the lighting itself is a commandment belonging to the woman, the mistress of the house. And Rabbi Yosef Chaim himself followed this practice in his own home, preparing and arranging the candles himself.
takeaways: Preparing the oil and wicks in advance is a fitting task for the husband, while the lighting itself belongs to the woman

paragraphs: Lo taqdim velo teacher; umin haddin yekola lehadliq achar sheyyaggia zeman arbit, dehaynu shaa urebia qodem hallayla beshaot zemanniyyot, abal qodem zeman zeh enah yekola lehadliq. umetzuvveh min hammubchar lehadliq chatzi shaa qodem sheqiat hachamma, veken nohagim bebetenu.

clarification.explanation: One should not light the Sabbath candles too early, nor too late. According to strict law one may light already from an hour and a quarter (in seasonal hours) before night — once the "time of the evening prayer" has arrived — but before this time it is forbidden to light. However, the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment (the recommended practice) is to light about half an hour before sunset, and this is how Rabbi Yosef Chaim practiced in his home.
takeaways: One may light from an hour and a quarter before the emergence of the stars; the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment is to light half an hour before sunset

paragraphs: Haishsha, lo chal aleha qabbalat-shabbat behadlaqat nerot shabbat ella ad shettesayyem kol hannerot asher madleqet bimqom hashshulchan sheshsham tihyeh habberaka shellah; veachar shettesayyem kol hannerot, tekep umiyyad tizroq miyyadah happetila shemmadleqet bah et hannerot, vetannicha yadah al eneha, vetaatzom eneha utebarek tekep. veyesh taam al-pi hassod baatzimat eneha otah shaa. veachar siyyum habberaka tiptach eneha vetireh zerichat or hannerot vehitpashshetut oran bammaqom hahu. veim hammaqom hu parus bo sedinin al haqqarqa, veenah yekola lizroq happetila baaretz, taamid echad etzlah kede shettekep umiyyad besiyyum hahadlaqa yiqqach happetila miyyadah vikabbenna. vedavqa haishsha tachul aleha qabbalat-shabbat behadlaqat hannerot shel shabbat, abal haanashim, im hem madliqim nerot shabbat beyadam, "p shemmebarekim alehem, lo tachul alehem qabbalat-shabbat ella kesheomerim "boi kaleh" v"mizmor shir leyom hashshabbat", vekaasher nebaer leqamman; velaken yekolim laasot melaka achar shemmadliqin; mihu, tob sheyyatnu beperush beet hahadlaqa sheen meqabbelim shabbat behadlaqat hanner.

clarification.explanation: For the woman, the acceptance of the Sabbath takes effect through the lighting of the Sabbath candles only after she has finished all the candles she lights in the place of the table (where her blessing is). Immediately upon finishing, she should throw down from her hand the wick she used to light, place her hand over her eyes and close them, and recite the blessing immediately (and there is a reason according to the esoteric tradition for closing her eyes at that moment); after the blessing she should open her eyes and see the light of the candles. If the floor is spread with sheets and she cannot throw the wick onto it, she should have someone stand near her to take the wick from her hand immediately and extinguish it. It is specifically the woman for whom the acceptance of the Sabbath takes effect through lighting; but men, even though they light and recite the blessing, do not accept the Sabbath through the lighting itself, but only when they say "Come, O bride" and "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" — and therefore they may still do work after lighting; nevertheless it is good that they explicitly state, at the time of lighting, that they are not thereby accepting the Sabbath.
takeaways: The woman accepts the Sabbath through lighting only after finishing all the candles; she then immediately throws down the wick, closes her eyes and recites the blessing (a matter of the esoteric tradition), and then opens her eyes to see the light

Men do not accept the Sabbath through lighting but only through "Come, O bride" and "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" — and may still do work afterward (though it is good to state this explicitly)

paragraphs: Nakon lehadliq achar shettachalip bigde shabbat; mihu, im ichara vechosheshet sheim tachalip begadeha lo yishshaer lah zeman lehadliq, az tukal lehadliq bebigde chol, veachar-kak tachalip begadeha. veim haishsha mitpallelet, tzarik shettitpallel mincha qodem hadlaqa velo achar hadlaqa, deha kebar qibbela shabbat bahadlaqa, veek titpallel shel chol. veraq arbit shel shabbat titpallel achar hahadlaqa.

clarification.explanation: It is proper to light the candles after the woman has already put on her Sabbath clothes. But if the hour is late and she is concerned that if she changes her clothes there will be no time left to light, she may light in her weekday clothes and change afterward. A woman who prays must pray the afternoon prayer before lighting, not after, since the moment she lights she has already accepted the Sabbath and can no longer pray a weekday prayer. Only the Sabbath evening prayer itself is prayed after the lighting.
takeaways: It is preferable to light after putting on Sabbath clothes, but if there is no time one lights first and changes afterward
The afternoon prayer must be prayed before lighting (since acceptance of the Sabbath takes effect afterward); the evening prayer is prayed only after lighting

paragraphs: Beshabbat mebarekin "lehadliq ner shel shabbat", vbyv"t mebarekin "lehadliq ner shel yv"t". upoh irenu nohagim hannashim lebarek byv"t "shehecheyanu" behadlaqat hanner, im hu yv"t sheomerim bo "shehecheyanu" beqiddush. vedavqa beshabbat katabnu lebarek achar hahadlaqa, abal byv"t mebarekin veaach"k madliqin; umeachar dbyv"t mebareket veaach"k madleqet, tzerika lehizzaher shello tasicha ad achar gemar kol hannerot shemmebareket alehem; veim shacha shello meinyan hahadlaqa: im adayin lo haddeleqa apillu ner echad, tachazor utebarek; veim qodem sheshshacha hidliqa ner echad meellu hannerot shebberaka alehem, lo tachazor utebarek.

clarification.explanation: On the Sabbath one recites the blessing "to light the Sabbath candle," and on a festival, "to light the festival candle." In Baghdad the women were accustomed to also recite "Who has kept us alive" at the time of lighting the candle on a festival, if it is a festival on which "Who has kept us alive" is said at Kiddush. There is an important difference in order: on the Sabbath the blessing is recited after the lighting (as mentioned above), but on a festival the blessing is recited before the lighting. Because of this, on a festival the woman must be careful not to speak until she has finished lighting all the candles over which the blessing was recited. If she spoke about something unrelated to the lighting: if she has not yet lit even one candle, she must go back and recite the blessing again; but if she had already managed to light one candle before speaking, she does not go back and recite the blessing again.
takeaways: On a festival the blessing is recited before the lighting (unlike the Sabbath), so one must be careful not to interrupt with speech until all the candles are lit
Interrupting with speech before even one candle is lit requires repeating the blessing; after one candle is lit, it does not

paragraphs: Shenayim veshalosh baale-battim sheokelim becheder echad kol echad al shulchano umadliqim sham, yaamod echad mehem lebarek ulehadliq veyaaseh kavvana al hashshear, veaz yadliqu al semak beraka shello. veim kebar qadam echad uberak vehidliq vehashshear lo shameu birkato, lo yebareku al nerot shellahem beshem umalkut, ella yebareku beli shem umalkut viharharu shem umalkut bilbabam, mippene deikka pelugta bazeh vesapeq berakot lehaqel. vekol zeh, im okelim vishenim sham beoto cheder, abal im raq okelim sham, vishenim kol echad becheder bipne atzmo, yadliqu hashshear kol echad bimqom shena vibarek; veim yirtzeh lehadliq bimqom akila, g"k yadliq belo beraka, veraq tzarik lehannicha shemen banner shemmadliq bimqom shena sheyyaspiq ad zeman sheyyabo lishon sham. ish veishto sheyyesh lahem ben nasuy, vehachammot madleqet umebareket bimqom hashshulchan, az tadliq kallatah bimqom shena shellah utebarek sham; veraq tizzaher lehannicha shemen sheyyaspiq ad et hashshena. veim tirtzeh hakkalla lehadliq bimqom hashshulchan, lo tebarek; meachar dachamotah hidliqa kebar ubereka.

clarification.explanation: When several heads of households eat in one room, each at his own table, and light candles there, only one of them should stand to recite the blessing and light, intending to include the others as well, and all of them may then light their candles relying on his blessing. If one has already recited the blessing and lit, and the others did not hear his blessing, they should not recite the blessing over their own candles with God's name and sovereignty, but only without it, having it in mind in their hearts, out of concern that there is a dispute on this matter and we are lenient in a doubt concerning blessings. All this applies when they both eat and sleep in the same room; but if they only eat together while each sleeps in his own room, each one lights and recites the blessing in his own sleeping place, and if he wants to also light in the place of eating, he lights there without a blessing, but must leave enough oil in the sleeping-place candle to last until he comes to sleep there. In a family with a mother-in-law and a daughter-in-law: if the mother-in-law has already recited the blessing and lit in the place of the table, the daughter-in-law lights and recites the blessing in her own sleeping place, and if she wants to also light in the place of the table, she does not recite a blessing, since the mother-in-law has already done so there.
takeaways: When several families eat in the same room, only one recites the blessing over the lighting for all of them
One who did not hear the blessing lights without God's name and sovereignty if he both eats and sleeps there; if he sleeps in a separate place, he recites the blessing himself there

paragraphs: Suma yekola lehadliq ulebarek al ner shabbat; umikkol maqom, im yesh lah baal piqqeach, nakon shehu yebarek veyadliq.

clarification.explanation: A blind woman may light and recite the blessing over the Sabbath candle herself. Nevertheless, if she has a sighted husband, it is right and proper that he be the one to light and recite the blessing in her place.
takeaways: A blind woman may light and recite the blessing over the Sabbath candle herself, but if there is a sighted husband, it is preferable that he light

paragraphs: Asur liga bener-shabbat shebbereku alayv achar shehudlaq, mippene shehuqtza lemitzvato, "p shezzeh hannogea lo qibbel shabbat adayin demuttar laasot melaka. vaapillu negia belo nidnud asur; velaken asur lehosip bo shemen; mihu, muttar lehadliq petila mishshalhebet dener-shabbat letzorek shabbat, kevan deeno nogea bappetila shel ner-shabbat.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to touch a Sabbath candle that has already had a blessing recited over it and has been lit, since it has been set aside (designated) for the fulfillment of its commandment — and this is so even if the one touching it has not yet himself accepted the Sabbath and is permitted to do other work. The prohibition against touching applies even to a light touch without any movement at all, and therefore it is also forbidden to add oil to the candle after it has been lit. Nevertheless, it is permitted to light another wick (an additional candle for the needs of the Sabbath) from the flame of the candle that is already lit, since in doing so one does not touch the wick of the Sabbath candle itself.
takeaways: It is forbidden to touch a lit Sabbath candle over which a blessing has been recited, even a light touch without movement, since it has been set aside for its commandment
It is permitted to use the flame of the candle to light another candle, as long as one does not touch the original wick

paragraphs: Yadliqu ner-shabbat bimqom hannachatam, velo yadliqum bezavit zo veyannichum bezavit acheret, apillu im zeh hammannicha umittaltela hu nakeri sheen lo issur muqtzeh; sheim yaasu ken, eno nikkar shehudlequ likbod shabbat. veken lo tadliqem beodam beyad hamsharet, vekol shekken shello tadliqem bachutz veyaknisum bipnim; vaapillu im haishsha chola, tzerika lehadliq nerot shabbat bimqom hannachatam.

clarification.explanation: One should light the Sabbath candles in the fixed place where they will remain, and should not light them in one corner and then move them to another — even if the one moving them is a non-Jew who is not subject to the prohibition of muktzeh — because if one does this, it will not be recognizable that they were lit in honor of the Sabbath. Likewise, one should not light the candles while they are still being held by a servant, and certainly it is forbidden to light them outside and then bring them inside. Even a sick woman must light the Sabbath candles specifically in the place where they will remain.
takeaways: The candles must be lit in the fixed place where they will remain — not lit and then moved — so that it is recognizable they were lit in honor of the Sabbath

paragraphs: Yadliqu nerot shabbat, rob hayyotze min happetila; sheim lo yadliq ella rosh happetila visalleq yado mimmenna, chashib keillu deleqa meeleha, veeno meqayyem metzuvveh bahadlaqa; veken haya benerot hammenora shel bet-hammiqdash; vetzarik lehizzaher bazeh gam benerot chanukka. utzerikin lehizzaher lekassot ervat haqqetannim bipne nerot shabbat shebbereku alehem.

clarification.explanation: When lighting Sabbath candles, one must light them so that most of the wick catches fire. If one lights only the tip of the wick and immediately removes his hand from it, this is considered as though the candle lit on its own, and he has not properly fulfilled the commandment. This was also the case with the candles of the Menorah in the Holy Temple. One must be careful about this also when lighting Chanukah candles. Additionally, one must be careful to cover the nakedness of small children in front of Sabbath candles over which a blessing has already been recited.
takeaways: One must light until most of the wick catches, not just the tip — this applies to Chanukah candles as well
One must be careful to cover the nakedness of small children in front of Sabbath candles that have already had a blessing recited over them

paragraphs: Shumman haalya achar shennimmocha, "p shehu nimshak achar happetila, gazeru bo chaza"l mishshum heka dela nimmocha, dehaynu, gezera shemma yabi chatikat alya veyannicha happetila betokah. laken im achar shennimmocha shumman haalya arab bo shemen kasher, kegon shemen zayit o shemen shumshemin vekayyotze, az muttar lehadliq bo. vehu haddin hacheleb sheqqorin bearbe "shechyam"(cheleb min hachay meubbad lehadlaqa), g"k dino ken demuttar lehadliq bo achar shennimmocha al-yede taarobet shemen acher kasher; veken qirbe dagim shennimmochu, gam-ken asur lehadliq bahem, veraq al-yede taarobet shemen kasher muttar; abal shemen shel besar haddagim atzman, dehaynu mah sheyyotze vezab min besar haddagim beet hattiggun bammachabat al haesh - im hu tzalul vetob, muttar lehadliq beli taarobet shemen acher. veshemen hammatzuy bapperas sheqqorin oto "dehen el karua", hare zeh pasul lehadliq bo apillu al-yede taarobet shemen kasher, ki zeh hu shemen-qiq deneesar bemishna aruka, depereshu baggemara lechad man deamar dehu qiqayon deyona, uperesh haramba"m, shehu shemen hanniqra "kera", vezeh pasul lekulle alema, ukemo shekkatebu happoseqim za"l.

clarification.explanation: Sheep-tail fat, after it has melted into a liquid and been absorbed into the wick, was forbidden by our Sages for lighting, as a decree — lest people come to use it before it melts and place an actual piece of fat inside the wick (which is certainly forbidden). Therefore, if, after the fat has melted, kosher oil (such as olive oil or sesame oil) was mixed into it, it is then permitted to light with the mixture. The same law applies to tallow from a living animal processed for lighting (called "shechim") — it is permitted only when mixed with kosher oil. Likewise, melted fish innards are forbidden unless mixed with kosher oil. But oil that comes out of the fish's own flesh during frying (if it is clear and good) may be used for lighting even without any mixture. A certain oil found in Persia ("dahn al-kara," castor oil) is forbidden for lighting under all circumstances, even mixed with kosher oil, since this is the oil explicitly forbidden in the Mishnah.
takeaways: Melted tail fat, tallow, or fish innards are permitted for lighting only when mixed with kosher oil
Castor oil ("dahn al-kara") is forbidden for lighting in all cases, even mixed with other oil

paragraphs: Im nimtza akbar met betok kad hashshemen, "p sheyyesh shishshim keneged haakbar, im oto hashshemen maus laakila, nipsal lehadlaqat nerot shabbat shemmebarekin alehem mishshum "haqribehu na lepechateka", abal muttar lehadliqo bishar meqomot shetztzarik lo ner bahem. vekatub beseper "tora lishmah": im hinnicha shemen zayit o shemen shumshemin, shehem reuyim laakila, tachat hammitta shora alehem rucha raa venipsalim laakila, velaken nipsalim lehadliq ner shabbat vener chanukka mishshum "haqribehu lepechateka", meachar dimis leadam baakila; abal shemen mar sheeno rauy laakila, enah shora alayv rucha raa umuttar lehadliqo bener shabbat vener chanukka.

clarification.explanation: A dead mouse found inside a jar of oil — even if there is sixty times the volume of the mouse present (so that the oil would technically be permitted for eating) — if that oil now appears repulsive for eating, it becomes invalid for lighting the Sabbath candles over which a blessing is recited, because of the principle of "Offer it now to your governor" (which forbids offering something repulsive to a commandment that one would not offer to a human king). But it is permitted to use this oil for lighting in other places in the house that need light. It is also brought that olive oil or sesame oil, fit for eating, that was placed under a bed — according to Torah Lishmah, an evil spirit rests upon it and it becomes invalid for eating, and consequently also invalid for lighting the Sabbath and Chanukah candles, for the same reason of "Offer it now to your governor." But bitter oil that was never fit for eating in the first place has no evil spirit resting upon it, and it is permitted to light the Sabbath and Chanukah candles with it.
takeaways: Oil that has become repulsive (such as from a dead mouse) is invalid for the Sabbath candle over which a blessing is recited, even if technically permitted for eating, because of "Offer it now to your governor"
Oil placed under a bed likewise becomes invalid for lighting, for the same reason, according to Torah Lishmah

paragraphs: Asur lehishtammesh leor hanner beshabbat, kol dabar shetztzarik iyyun harbeh, kegon lepallot begadayv o liqrot beseper, apillu eno motzi mippiv mah sheqqore; gezera shemma yishkach veyatteh hanner leqareb hashshemen el happetila kede shettadliq yapeh. veyesh mattirim bener shaava o shel cheleb hakkaruk sebib happetila sheen derek lehattoto; veyesh oserin gam bazeh, gezera shemma yimchat rosh happetila sheyyesh bazeh kibbuy. vekatebu haacharonim za"l, deen limchot beyad hammeqillin bener shaava hakkaruk sebib happetila, deyesh lahem al mah sheyyismoku; al-ken yesh lehattir bikhay gavna letzorek metzuvveh, dehaynu lilmod tora vei epshar lo sheyyannicha shomer alayv leshamero; abal im epshar lo lehannicha shomer, en lismok lehattir apillu bener shel shaava o cheleb hakkaruk sebib happetila. veda, sheyyesh nerot cheleb kerukkin sebib happetila sheenam maaseh umman, veellu tzerikin limchot tamid kol zeman deliqatam, vekaasher anachnu roim bechush, hinneh beellu en lehattir. veken nerot zekukit shemmannichin bahem mayim, veshemen al hammayim, vehappetila doleqet beemtza hanner, "g deellu lo shayyak bahem hattaya - yesh bahem mechitta, velaken gam ellu asurin. v"g deamarnu sheyyesh lismok al hammattirin bener shaava o cheleb hakkaruk al happetila deen derek limchot otam, beheka dei epshar lo lehannicha shomer, im kol zeh yere shamayim, im epshar lo lehannicha ner shaava hannizkar betok keli zekukit sheyyesh bo petach, vesoger happetach meereb shabbat bemanul barzel veyimsor hammapteach beyad adam acher, o sheyyisgor happetach beqesher meshunneh - yaaseh kak, kede leqayyem gezerat chaza"l beli piqpuq. veayyen b"machaziq beraka" ub"chiqre-leb", mahdura batera; veayyen "machatzit-hashsheqel", resh si' r"h, ushear acharonim mah shekkatebu bedabar zeh.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to use the light of a candle on the Sabbath for anything requiring much scrutiny, such as checking clothes or reading a book — even reading silently — out of concern that one might, out of absorption, forget and tilt the candle to bring the oil closer to the wick to brighten the light, thereby transgressing the prohibition of kindling on the Sabbath. Some permit this with special candles (wax or tallow wound around the wick) that cannot be tilted, but others disagree, out of concern that one might need to trim the tip of the wick ("le-mechot"), an action considered forbidden extinguishing. The halachic authorities ruled that one should not protest against those lenient with such wax candles, and therefore it is permitted to be lenient in such a case for the sake of a commandment (such as Torah study) when it is not possible to have a watchman present. But if a watchman can be arranged, one should not rely on the leniency even with wax candles. One must also be careful: plain tallow candles (not skillfully made) that require frequent trimming should not be treated leniently at all; and likewise glass candles with water and oil, where the wick burns in the middle — even though there is no concern of tilting, there is a need for trimming, and therefore these too are forbidden. One who fears Heaven, even when permitted to be lenient with a wax candle, should preferably place the candle in a locked glass vessel and give the key to another person, in order to fulfill the Sages' decree without any doubt.
takeaways: It is forbidden to read anything requiring much scrutiny by candlelight on the Sabbath, out of concern that one might tilt the candle
A wax or tallow candle wound around the wick (which cannot be tilted) may be relied upon only when no watchman can be arranged, and not with glass candles or plain candles that require trimming

paragraphs: Mah sheaseru chaza"l leor hanner - apillu im hanner gabohha kamma qomot sheeno maggia elayv, name asur mishshum dela pelug rabbanan bigzeratam. veim shenayim qorin beinyan echad, beyachad, beseper echad – muttar; abal im kol echad topes seper bipne atzmo, "p sheqqorin beinyan echad, asur, dekol chad tarud leayyen besipro veeno margish bemaaseh chabero im yabo lehattot kede sheyyimnaehu. veyesh meqillin beqorin beinyan echad apillu im kol echad topes seper bipne atzmo, veyesh lismok al zeh bishat haddechaq, ki ledina, haiqqar kisbara rishona deoserin gam bazeh. veim echad qore leor hanner umannicha etzlo shomer sheomer lo: ten daatka alay shello atteh! hare zeh muttar lekulle alema, vaapillu leishto yakol lehannichah shomeret alayv.

clarification.explanation: The prohibition of using candlelight applies even if the candle is so high up that one cannot physically reach it, since the Sages did not distinguish between different situations in their decree. If two people are reading the same subject together from one shared book, it is permitted, since each one would notice if the other were about to tilt the candle and would stop him. But if each holds a separate book, even on the same subject, it is forbidden, since each is absorbed in his own book and would not notice his companion's action. Some are lenient even in the case of separate books on the same subject, in a time of pressing need, though the primary ruling is to be stringent. If a person is reading alone by candlelight but has a watchman beside him who explicitly says, "Pay attention to me, so that I don't tilt it!" — this is permitted according to all opinions, and even his own wife may serve as this watchman.
takeaways: Two people reading from one shared book on the same subject is permitted; from two separate books it is forbidden (except in pressing need)
With an explicit watchman whose role is to ensure the candle is not tilted, one may read alone by candlelight, even if the watchman is his wife

paragraphs: Qeria shehaadam ragil bah harbeh, kegon mizmore tehillim leadam haragil bahem, vekol-shekken mizmore shabbat, veken qeria sheqqorin qodem qiddush shehurgal bah bekol lel-shabbat, veken arbaa peraqim shel mishna deshabbat harishonim sheragil leomeram al hashshulchan bekol lel-shabbat, veeno tzarik bekol ellu leayyen beseper ella rashe peraqim, hare zeh muttar liqrot lebaddo leor hanner, kevan deeno tzarik leayyen bahem kol kak leor hanner sheyyihyeh yapeh kede shita, vaapillu beor qal saggi leh. veken hahaggada belel-pesach shechal beshabbat deragil bah ushegura bepiv, muttar liqrot. vehu haddin leshir-hashshirim lemi sheragil bahem, veken tepilla shel shacharit shehu seder haqqarebbanot, umizmorim deragil bahem, muttar liqrot leor hanner lebaddo beli shomer. umah shehittir haggaon yaabe"tz za"l by"ch pirqe mishna lehargil bahem, la modena leh bazeh.

clarification.explanation: A reading that a person is very familiar with and does not require close examination — such as psalms one is accustomed to, and certainly the Sabbath psalms, sections customarily recited before Kiddush, the first four chapters of tractate Shabbat customarily recited at the table every Sabbath night, the Passover Haggadah when Passover falls on the Sabbath (for one fluent in it), the Song of Songs for one accustomed to it, and the order of sacrifices and psalms of the morning prayer that one is accustomed to — may be read alone by candlelight without a watchman, since he only needs a glance at the beginnings of the sections rather than close examination, and there is therefore no concern that he will tilt the candle to brighten the light. However, Rabbi Yosef Chaim disagrees with the Gaon Rabbi Yaavetz, who permitted this even for eighteen chapters of Mishnah that one is accustomed to, and holds that one should be stringent about this.
takeaways: Familiar reading that requires no close examination (Tehillim, familiar prayer sections) is permitted alone by candlelight without a watchman
Rabbi Yosef Chaim disagrees with extending this leniency to eighteen chapters of Mishnah, and holds that one should be stringent

paragraphs: Kelim haddomim zeh lazeh vetzarik iyyun rab lehabchin ben zeh lazeh, asur lebadeqan leor hanner, abal mistakkel hu bemah shebbakkos ubiqara leor hanner, shehittiru lo mippene hanneqiyyut umippene hassakkana, vekol kol kayyotze bazeh. ukeli mareh hashshaot: im hareshimot shel hashshaot vehaddaqqim qetannim meod shetztzarik lahem iyyun rab lehekkeram, asur lirotam leor hanner; abal im gassim meat sheen tzarik lahem iyyun rab, muttar. vetzitziyyot hamsuksakim umeurbabim harbeh vetzarik iyyun rab lehapridam ulebidqam, asur lehapridam ulebidqam; abal enam mesuksakim, shari; veayyen "maamar mareddekay" za"l.

clarification.explanation: Utensils that resemble one another, requiring much careful scrutiny to distinguish between them, are forbidden to be examined by candlelight. But one may look at what is inside a cup or a bowl by candlelight, which was permitted out of concern for cleanliness (to make sure there is no dirt in them) and out of concern for danger, and similarly for anything like this. Regarding clocks: if the markings of the hours and minutes are very small and require much scrutiny, it is forbidden to look at them by candlelight; but if the markings are coarse and do not require special scrutiny, it is permitted. Likewise, tzitzit strings that are very tangled and mixed together, requiring much scrutiny to separate and check them, may not be checked by candlelight; but if they are not so tangled, it is permitted.
takeaways: Distinguishing between similar utensils that requires much scrutiny is forbidden by candlelight; a general glance (for cleanliness or safety) is permitted
The rule: the more concentration and time something requires to discern, the greater the concern about tilting the candle, and therefore it is forbidden
